photo.alt: Conestoga wagon in front of Eagle Rock

stli.description: Cross the harbor toward the Statue of Liberty, France's gift dedicated in 1886. The island setting brings an enduring symbol of freedom into view against the skyline and waters of New York.

photo.alt: Patina green statue atop her pedestal on Liberty Island; grey cloudy sky in the distance

ston.description: Explore the Greenwich Village streets associated with the Stonewall Uprising of June 1969. This small urban landscape marks a pivotal moment in the LGBTQ civil rights movement.

photo.alt: Pink, purple and white tulips blooming in a park

sucr.description: Walk beside dark lava flows left by an eruption roughly a thousand years ago. Trees and flowers growing among the volcanic rock reveal the gradual renewal of a landscape that changed lives across northern Arizona.

photo.alt: a cinder cone volcano and ponderosa pine trees

tica.description: Climb into mountain scenery before entering a hidden world of decorated cave chambers. Guided tours connect delicate formations with the science and history of cave exploration.

photo.alt: Twisty helictites growing off a stalactite

tont.description: Look into cliff dwellings occupied between 1300 and 1450 in the northern Sonoran Desert. The buildings preserve evidence of the diverse communities that formed the Salado cultural world in Tonto Basin.

photo.alt: cliff dwelling in the spring with desert plants and wildflowers.

tule.description: Explore the history of the Tule Lake Segregation Center, where Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II. Nearby Camp Tulelake adds the stories of a CCC camp, detention facility, and prisoner-of-war camp.

photo.alt: White house with a concrete deck and flag poll in the front.

tusk.description: Explore an open fossil landscape at the edge of Las Vegas, shaped by water over roughly 570,000 years. The ground beneath today's desert preserves evidence of changing environments and ancient life.

photo.alt: Tule Springs during winter

tuzi.description: Explore the remains of a hilltop pueblo above the Verde Valley. Its growth from a small community about a thousand years ago reveals the importance of water and farming in this desert landscape.

photo.alt: A marsh with open water, cattails, and a masonry dwelling beyond.

waco.description: See the fossil story of a nursery herd of Columbian mammoths preserved in central Texas. These animals stood as tall as 14 feet, giving an arresting sense of the Ice Age world beneath today's landscape.

photo.alt: Visitors view fossils from walkway
photo.credit: NPS Photo 【4†Image: Entrance sign to Waco Mammoth.】 Waco Mammoth National Monument became part of the National Park Service on July 10, 2015.

waca.description: Follow a winding canyon landscape where ancestral communities built homes beneath cliffs and farmed along the rim. The surviving dwellings connect dramatic scenery with Indigenous lives and continuing cultural ties.

photo.alt: Walnut Canyon's cliff dwellings are illuminated by the afternoon sun.

wupa.description: Explore stone pueblos between the Painted Desert and northern Arizona's pine-covered highlands. In the early 1100s, ancestors of today's Pueblo communities made this a center of trade and cultural life.

photo.alt: a large stone pueblo in a desert beneath mostly sunny skies with mountains in background

yuho.description: Explore the setting of a large, unexcavated pueblo in Montezuma Valley between Mesa Verde and Ute Mountain. Protected since 1919, Yucca House preserves an archaeological landscape whose scale emerges through careful observation.

photo.alt: Cattails with mesa in background.

alpo.description: Explore the mountain railroad that completed Pennsylvania's canal route between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh in 1834. Its surviving landscape reveals the ingenuity required to carry boats and travelers across the Alleghenies.

photo.alt: Engine House and tavern

ande.description: Walk the grounds of the Civil War prison where nearly 13,000 men died. The cemetery and National Prisoner of War Museum broaden this place of remembrance to the experience of American captivity across conflicts.

photo.alt: A cannon sits out in front of a replica of part of the wooden stockade walls once at Andersonville

anjo.description: Explore the home and community of Andrew Johnson, whose presidency unfolded amid the struggle over Reconstruction. His story brings impeachment, citizenship, and the balance of federal powers into a personal historic setting.

photo.alt: Andrew Johnson Homestead with snow

beol.description: Step into a reconstructed adobe trading post on the Santa Fe Trail beside the Arkansas River. Bent's Fort reveals the exchange among traders, travelers, Cheyenne and Arapaho people, and the expanding United States during the 1840s.

photo.alt: A group of visitors stand around a large wooden apparatus in a plaza courtyard.

boaf.description: Walk Beacon Hill streets shaped by Boston's nineteenth-century Black community. Historic places connect abolition, the Underground Railroad, and the long struggle for equal education and civil rights.

photo.alt: View from the pulpit at the African Meeting House, which has rows of benches and an upper gallery

brvb.description: Explore the people and communities whose organizing led to the landmark Brown v. Board of Education decision. The site reveals how ordinary families challenged school segregation and helped change the nation's understanding of equality.

photo.alt: Brown v Board National Historical Park

carl.description: Explore the home and mountain setting of writer Carl Sandburg. The farm landscape offers a personal view of the poet's life, work, and connection to the natural world.

photo.alt: A view of Sandburg's study as visitors see it today

cawo.description: Visit the home where historian Carter G. Woodson helped transform the study of African American life. Here he established Negro History Week in 1926, the observance that developed into Black History Month.

photo.alt: The restored facades of three historic Victorian row-homes on an urban street in Washington, DC

chpi.description: Explore Snee Farm, a plantation associated with Constitution signer Charles Pinckney. The site examines his political life alongside the labor and lives of the African people he enslaved.

photo.alt: 1828 Lowcountry cottage and grounds

clba.description: Explore the home where Clara Barton spent the final fifteen years of her life. Its unusual spaces reveal a life organized around humanitarian service and aid during war and disaster.

photo.alt: two and half story wooden frame house with double porch and stone corner posts.

edal.description: Step into the modest house of Edgar Allan Poe during his productive Philadelphia years. The rooms offer a close view of the creativity, family hardship, and uncertainty behind his enduring stories.

photo.alt: Color photo showing a large raven statue with wings outspread on a metal plinth.

eise.description: Explore Dwight and Mamie Eisenhower's farm beside the Gettysburg battlefield, with views toward South Mountain. This country retreat also became a meeting place for world leaders during the tensions of the Cold War.

photo.alt: The Eisenhower home with Ike's putting green in the foreground

elro.description: Explore Val-Kill, Eleanor Roosevelt's home and a gathering place for activists, journalists, friends, and state visitors. Its informal setting opens a personal view of her public life and commitment to human rights.

photo.alt: Val-Kill Cottage in the Summer

euon.description: Explore Tao House, the secluded California home where Eugene O'Neill wrote several of his best-known plays. The hillside setting connects a quiet refuge with the intense family worlds of his later work.

photo.alt: Eugene O'Neill Home in Danville, California

fila.description: Explore Ida Saxton McKinley's historic home and the stories of America's first ladies in downtown Canton. The site examines how the role grew from a private relationship into a position of public influence.

photo.alt: a front view of the Ida Saxton McKinley House
photo.credit: NPS Photo 【4†Image: A piano in the Saxton McKinley Home】 Ida Saxton's original piano is just one of many items belonging to President McKinley and First Lady Ida McKinley.

foth.description: Visit the theater where Abraham Lincoln was shot on April 14, 1865. The surrounding historic places connect his assassination with the ordinary people who witnessed and responded to a national tragedy.

photo.alt: Picture of the front of Ford's Theatre

fobo.description: Follow a three-mile loop through the landscape of Fort Bowie and Apache Pass. The route reveals the collision between Chiricahua Apache defense of their homeland and the U.S. Army's westward expansion.

photo.alt: Ruins of the fort with mountains and valley in the background.

foda.description: Explore the surviving buildings of a frontier post that guarded routes across west Texas from 1854 to 1891. The setting beneath rugged cliffs brings the military and travel history of the Trans-Pecos into view.

photo.alt: Garrison Flag flying over the post.

fola.description: Walk a post that began as an 1834 fur-trading fort and became a major Northern Plains military center. Its buildings and grounds connect western migration with treaties, conflict, and Indigenous resistance to encroachment.

photo.alt: A large two story white building with pillars. Several windows with green shutters

fols.description: Explore a well-preserved sandstone army post from the 1860s and 1870s beside the Santa Fe Trail. Barracks and other historic buildings reveal military life during a turbulent era of expansion and conflict.

photo.alt: Men in 19th century U.S. Army uniforms fire a reproduction period cannon.

fopo.description: Explore vaulted brick casemates directly beneath the Golden Gate Bridge. Built to defend San Francisco Bay after the Gold Rush, Fort Point pairs intricate military architecture with an extraordinary harbor setting.

photo.alt: Fort Point with visitors approaching on road in front and Golden Gate Bridge above.

fora.description: Explore Roanoke Island's layered history, from Algonquian communities and early English colonization to a Civil War freedmen's community. The wooded coastal setting also holds stories of later experiments in radio communication.

photo.alt: An earthworks covered in reddish-green grass about 4 feet high in a star pattern

fosc.description: Walk among historic buildings, a parade ground, and tallgrass prairie at a post active through the upheavals of 1842–1873. Its stories connect westward expansion, contested freedom, and the Civil War.

photo.alt: Picture of the post hospital with the parade ground and trees in the background.

fosm.description: Explore the edge of historic Indian Territory through military remains, courthouse stories, and the Trail of Tears. The site follows nearly eighty years of conflict, law, and federal power from 1817 to 1896.

photo.alt: Aerial view of visitor center

fous.description: Explore a reconstructed trading post where Northern Plains nations exchanged buffalo robes and furs for goods from across the world. Active from 1828 to 1867, Fort Union reveals the relationships that sustained Upper Missouri commerce.

photo.alt: View from Missouri River bottoms of Southwest bastion

fova.description: Explore Columbia River history through a fur-trading post, military places, and aviation stories. The park's separate sites reveal transitions in settlement, power, and community across the Pacific Northwest.

photo.alt: Fort Vancouver Garden

frdo.description: Explore Cedar Hill, where Frederick Douglass lived for the final seventeen years of his life. The hilltop home brings his work as an abolitionist, writer, and advocate for equality into a personal setting.

photo.alt: Visitors take photos in front of a historic house

frla.description: Explore the home and design office where Frederick Law Olmsted established his landscape architecture practice in 1883. The site reveals how ideas and drawings became parks and public landscapes across the country.

photo.alt: Fairsted
photo.credit: NPS Photo 【4†Image: Dark wood box with four shallow drawers on large wooden table with blueprint】 A box of colored pencils and a draftsmen's handbook sit on a table in the drafting room. These materials reflect the period during which Frederick Law Olmsted, Jr. was the senior partner in the Brookline, MA landscape architecture firm.

frhi.description: Explore Albert Gallatin's restored country estate above the Monongahela River. Its rooms and grounds introduce the Treasury secretary whose work helped finance the Louisiana Purchase, exploration, and early national infrastructure.

photo.alt: front view of historical Stone House and Visitor Center with green grass lawn with trees and clouds

grko.description: Explore the headquarters of a cattle operation that once ranged across a ten-million-acre empire. Historic ranch buildings and open land reveal the labor and business behind a powerful image of the American West.

photo.alt: A front view of the ranch house.

hamp.description: Explore the surviving estate of a plantation that once extended across 25,000 acres. Its grand house and working landscape reveal the intertwined lives of the Ridgely family, enslaved people, servants, and other laborers.

photo.alt: Hampton Mansion in the fall

hstr.description: Explore the Missouri surroundings that Harry Truman knew before, during, and after his presidency. Home and neighborhood stories connect an internationally consequential public life with familiar routines and local roots.

photo.alt: The Truman home near sunset.

heho.description: Explore Herbert Hoover's modest birthplace and the community landscape preserved around it. The site traces the early influences behind a life of humanitarian service and a presidency marked by crisis.

photo.alt: A one story wood frame house has board-and-batten exterior siding and a picket fence painted white.

hofr.description: Explore Franklin D. Roosevelt's family home in the Hudson Valley, a refuge he returned to through personal and political crises. Gardens, paths, and nearby presidential history place his long public career within a familiar landscape.

photo.alt: A stucco and fieldstone house with white trim and circular portico.

hofu.description: Explore 848 acres around a charcoal-fired ironmaking community that operated from 1771 to 1883. Historic structures reveal the technology, business, and everyday work behind early American industry.

photo.alt: Melted iron pouring into a mold from a metal bucket.

hutr.description: Step into a trading post that has sold goods and traded Native American art in Ganado since 1878. Wooden floors, rugs, and mercantile spaces connect a working business with the history of the Navajo Nation.

photo.alt: Spring lambs with their Navajo-Churro ewe.

jaga.description: Explore the home whose front porch became the stage for James Garfield's 1880 presidential campaign. The house opens the story of his family and a political career cut short by assassination.

photo.alt: Front porch of Garfield home showing red front door

jofi.description: Explore the birthplace of John F. Kennedy in a residential Boston-area neighborhood. The family home introduces the early surroundings of a child who would become the thirty-fifth president.

photo.alt: John Fitzgerald Kennedy National Historic Site

jomu.description: Explore John Muir's home and fruit-ranch landscape, where family life and working land shaped a passionate advocate for wilderness. The site connects his writing and conservation work with the practical world he inhabited.

photo.alt: White two story house capped by a bell tower and ringed with palm trees

knri.description: Explore village ground beside the Knife River where earthlodge communities farmed, hunted, and traded. The site reveals centuries of Indigenous commerce before and during the rise of the fur trade.

photo.alt: Summer view of Earthlodge
photo.credit: NPS photo 【4†Image: Interior View of Earthlodge】 Interior View of Earthlodge

liho.description: Walk the neighborhood around Abraham and Mary Lincoln's Springfield home. The preserved domestic setting brings the future president into view as a spouse, parent, and neighbor.

photo.alt: The two-story, tan Lincoln Home with a rainbow in the sky above it.

chsc.description: Encounter the school where the Little Rock Nine challenged segregation in 1957. The site examines their courage and the confrontation that tested the federal government's commitment to civil rights.

photo.alt: The front facade of Little Rock Central High School

long.description: Explore a Georgian house that served as Washington's Revolutionary headquarters and later the home of poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. Its layered history also includes colonial enslavement and community activism.

photo.alt: Yellow three-story mansion with symmetrical facade. Steps and large lawn in foreground. Framed by br
photo.credit: NPS Photo / James P. Jones | Photography RI

mawa.description: Explore the preserved home of Maggie Lena Walker in Richmond's historic Jackson Ward. Her work as a bank president, editor, and organizer reveals a determined campaign for economic opportunity and civil rights under Jim Crow.

photo.alt: Maggie L. Walker's home and adjacent buildings

manz.description: Explore the Owens Valley site where the U.S. government incarcerated Japanese Americans during World War II. Surviving traces and reconstructed spaces help reveal the lives disrupted behind the camp's boundaries.

photo.alt: People walk to barracks framed by mountain peaks.

mava.description: Explore Martin Van Buren's home and historic landscape near his birthplace. The setting invites a closer look at a political life shaped by expansion, Indigenous removal, slavery, and the crises leading toward the Civil War.

photo.alt: Lindenwald, a yellow, 3 story mansion, is surrounded by trees.

mabe.description: Explore the council house associated with Mary McLeod Bethune and the National Council of Negro Women. The site connects Black women's organizing with the struggle for civil rights and expanded opportunity.

photo.alt: MAMC

miin.description: Walk the Idaho landscape where more than 13,000 Japanese Americans were held during World War II. Remnants of the camp preserve personal histories and the consequences of incarceration without due process.

photo.alt: Origami cranes twirl on carousel

mimi.description: Explore the Cold War missile landscape hidden in the open Great Plains. Preserved facilities reveal the technology, daily vigilance, and immense destructive power behind nuclear deterrence.

photo.alt: Glass structure over the silo allows visitors to look down at the missile

nico.description: Explore a Great Plains community established by formerly enslaved African Americans seeking opportunity after Reconstruction. Historic buildings preserve the story of Black homesteading and a settlement whose community endures.

photo.alt: A group of people watching people on horseback during a parade

nisi.description: Explore the remains of a South Carolina backcountry town, trading place, and Revolutionary battlefield. The landscape reveals the competing ambitions of settlers, Cherokee people, and armies in the eighteenth century.

photo.alt: A cannon is in the left foreground with the Maham rifle tower in the distance.

paav.description: Walk the ceremonial avenue where Americans have paraded, protested, and marked national change. Its streetscape connects the everyday capital with the public rituals and political struggles of the nation.

photo.alt: Motorcycles pass by a crowd in a parade.
photo.credit: NPS 【4†Image: A stone plaza depicting a map of the globe.】 Explore the plaza, fountains, and artwork of the US Navy Memorial.

wicl.description: Explore the Arkansas house where Bill Clinton spent his earliest years with his mother and grandparents. The setting introduces the family and community experiences behind the future president's public life.

photo.alt: The birthplace home of President Bill Clinton illuminated at dusk.

rrbh.description: Explore the Illinois home associated with Ronald Reagan's boyhood. The house connects a small-town upbringing with the early life of the future actor and president.

photo.alt: Draft image from the Ronald Reagan Boyhood Home operator's visitor page
photo.credit: Young America's Foundation; exact photographer not established

sahi.description: Explore Theodore Roosevelt's home, historic buildings, and 83 acres of natural surroundings. His family retreat became a Summer White House, linking a Long Island landscape with the affairs of a growing world power.

photo.alt: A large house painted gray with green lawn and trees.

sapa.description: Explore a colonial churchyard and stone church drawn into the American Revolution. The grounds connect local voting and militia life with the troops who used the unfinished chapel as a wartime hospital.

photo.alt: Rebecca Turner gravesite

sama.description: Walk nine acres of historic waterfront with wharves and buildings tied to New England's maritime past. Salem's preserved places connect local work and commerce with stories reaching across the world's oceans.

photo.alt: A three mast tall ship on the water under a blue sky with red brick buildings on the shore.

sand.description: Pause beside the landscape where U.S. troops attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho encampment on November 29, 1864. The site preserves a place of profound loss, remembrance, and continuing importance to descendant communities.

photo.alt: Four white Indian lodges on a grassy plain.

sair.description: Explore twelve acres beside the Saugus River where seventeenth-century ironmakers brought industrial skills to colonial Massachusetts. Waterwheels, forges, and mills reveal the mechanics and labor of early iron production.

photo.alt: Several wooden structures amid green fields and trees under partly cloudy sky and beside river.

spar.description: Explore the armory landscape and collections behind nearly two centuries of military manufacturing. Firearms, historic buildings, and engineering stories reveal how Springfield influenced both national defense and American industry.

photo.alt: The Main Arsenal

stea.description: Explore massive steam locomotives and the spaces where railroads were built, repaired, and preserved. Steamtown connects the machinery's scale with the workers and travelers who shaped the railway age.

photo.alt: large black train with number 6039 painted in white lettering, sitting on turntable track

thrb.description: Explore the Manhattan townhouse setting of Theodore Roosevelt's childhood. His early interests and efforts to overcome poor health reveal the beginnings of a lifelong enthusiasm for vigorous outdoor life.

photo.alt: A Victorian-era parlor with blue wallpaper and blue carpeting.

thri.description: Visit the Buffalo house where an improvised ceremony brought Theodore Roosevelt into the presidency in 1901. The setting introduces the sudden transition and the policies that would reshape government and international affairs.

photo.alt: Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural Site

thst.description: Explore the home landscape of Thomas Stone, a Maryland signer of the Declaration of Independence. The estate connects a consequential political decision with the family and property he risked in supporting independence.

photo.alt: 5 part Mansion at Haberdeventure
photo.credit: NPS Photo / Stephen Girimont 【4†Image: Small family cemetery with grave markers】 Stone Family Cemetery

tuai.description: Explore Moton Field, where African American military pilots began their flight training during World War II. Hangars and exhibits reveal the skill and determination behind the airmen who challenged the assumptions of a segregated military.

photo.alt: Red-Tail P-51D Mustang In Flight Exhibit

tuin.description: Explore the campus story that Booker T. Washington began building in 1881. Historic places connect education and self-determination with George Washington Carver's agricultural research and Tuskegee's continuing influence.

photo.alt: A three story Queen Anne Revival style red brick house

ulsg.description: Explore White Haven, the Dent family home where Ulysses S. Grant met Julia and later lived with his family. The site examines their lives alongside those of the enslaved African Americans who worked the property.

photo.alt: Green sided, two story house with green trees

vama.description: Explore a grand Hudson Valley estate built for the Vanderbilts' privileged way of life. The mansion and grounds reveal the architecture, wealth, and social world of America's Gilded Age.

photo.alt: Misty April Morning
photo.credit: NPS Photo/Bill Urbin 【4†Image: Fall Colors in the Hudson Valley】 Thousands of visitors flock to the Hudson Valley in the Fall to see the leaves change colors.

waba.description: Walk the landscape where Custer's cavalry attacked Peace Chief Black Kettle's Cheyenne village at dawn on November 27, 1868. The site offers a place to remember those killed and examine the Great Plains Wars.

photo.alt: Cheyenne tipis backlite by sunset

whmi.description: Explore the place where a mission encounter became part of a devastating transformation of Cayuse homelands. The site examines newcomers, disease, conflict, and the consequences that followed the killings of 1847.

photo.alt: A tipi sits beneath a tree near a walking trail

wiho.description: Explore the hilltop Greek Revival house where William Howard Taft was born and grew up. Family rooms and stories reveal the civic values and early environment of a future president and chief justice.

photo.alt: A yellow two-story brick building with tall windows and green shutters on them

cato.description: Explore wooded mountain trails in a landscape restored through New Deal-era public works. Rocky viewpoints and regrowing forest reveal how former working land became a place for recreation.

photo.alt: Rock formation with mountains in the background

coga.description: Pause among trees, lawn, and water within the National Mall's memorial landscape. Constitution Gardens offers a quieter setting for reflection close to the capital's major monuments.

photo.alt: Shot of the Garden Pond with the Washington Monument in the background

fowa.description: Explore a Potomac River fort whose defenses evolved from nineteenth-century masonry to twentieth-century concrete and steel. Its commanding riverside position reveals why this approach to Washington mattered for more than two centuries.

photo.alt: Entrance way into historic Fort Washington
photo.credit: NPS Photo 【4†Image: Fort Washington Volunteers firing a cannon】 Fort Washington Guard fires one of the park's cannons. Demonstrations are presented during the summer months April-October.

gree.description: Follow forest paths and camp among trees just beyond Washington's urban core. Greenbelt offers a wooded setting for walking and overnight stays close to the capital.

photo.alt: Tent in the Greenbelt Park campground

naca.description: Explore park places across the nation's capital, from neighborhood green spaces to landscapes tied to public memory. This retained inventory entry represents a broad park grouping rather than one entrance or visitor destination.

photo.alt: The red barns and outbuildings at Oxon Hill Farm

mall.description: Walk the capital's broad ceremonial landscape between museums, monuments, and spaces used for national gatherings. The National Mall brings commemoration, protest, and everyday public life into the same open setting.

photo.alt: Aerial of the west side of National Mall and Memorial Parks

pisc.description: Follow boardwalks over freshwater tidal wetlands and paths through meadows and woods beside the Potomac. Habitat for bald eagles, ospreys, and beavers shares the landscape with National Colonial Farm.

photo.alt: Building at National Colonial Farm at Piscataway Park

prwi.description: Explore wooded trails and streams in a park that began as a Depression-era recreation area in 1936. The forest connects the legacy of children's relief camps with generations of walking, cycling, and camping.

photo.alt: An original 1930's sign for Chopawamsic National Recreational Demonstration Area

rocr.description: Explore 1,754 acres of wooded valley within the capital, protected as a federal park in 1890. Creekside paths and old trees offer a close encounter with nature and layers of human history inside the city.

photo.alt: Stone bridge and fall leaves

whho.description: Explore the public landscape around the White House, a presidential home and a longstanding focus for protest and national debate. President's Park connects the building's familiar image with the people who have lived, worked, and gathered here.

photo.alt: Crowds of people populate the White House South Lawn on a sunny day with the White House in view

wotr.description: Pair a performance with a park setting of wooded grounds and outdoor gathering spaces. Wolf Trap brings music, theater, and dance into a national park devoted to the performing arts.

photo.alt: The Filene Center House full of patrons

appa.description: Follow a footpath extending more than 2,190 miles through the Appalachian Mountains, from wooded valleys to open ridges. Built by private citizens and completed in 1937, the trail offers both short walks and long-distance journeys.

photo.alt: Silhouette of a man with backpack standing on McAfee Knob at sunset with mountains in the distance.

cajo.description: Explore more than 3,000 miles of Chesapeake Bay water trails linking Indigenous homelands with the voyages John Smith recorded in 1608. Shoreline stops and paddling routes reveal a world of communities, waterways, and continuing Tribal connections.

photo.alt: A heron at sunset in the waters and marshes of Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge

iatr.description: Follow a roughly 1,200-mile route through Wisconsin's glacial landscapes. Ridges, lakes, and valleys reveal the edge of the last great ice sheet across the ancestral lands of fifteen Tribes.

photo.alt: Photograph of a large glacial erratic boulder in autumn with trees covered in colorful foliage and f

lecl.description: Trace nearly 4,900 miles from Pittsburgh toward the Pacific along routes associated with the 1803–1806 Lewis and Clark expedition. Connected places reveal both the travelers' journey and the homelands of more than sixty Tribal nations.

photo.alt: Small waterfall with brown rocks and green moss

noco.description: Explore a route of more than 4,800 miles from North Dakota to Vermont through northern forests, open prairie, and lake country. Individual trail sections reveal glacial landscapes, communities, and a remarkable variety of walking terrain.

photo.alt: Hiking on trail

semo.description: Trace the 54-mile route of the 1965 voting rights march from Selma to Montgomery. Interpretive places connect the roads and river crossing with the people whose nonviolent campaign challenged racial exclusion.

photo.alt: 50th Anniversary Walking Classroom Participants.

bicy.description: Explore more than 729,000 acres of freshwater swamp that help sustain the neighboring Everglades and coastal estuaries. Cypress country and mixed plant communities provide habitat for the endangered Florida panther.

photo.alt: A small alligator basking on top of dry vegetation.

bith.description: Explore more than 113,000 acres where longleaf pine forest, cypress-lined bayous, and other southeast Texas habitats meet. Trails and waterways reveal a biological crossroads that includes insect-eating pitcher plants and sundews.

photo.alt: Reflections of twisting tupelo trees in calm water below a green canopy.

crmp.description: Explore the wider volcanic landscape adjoining Craters of the Moon's developed monument area. Lava flows, cinder cones, and sagebrush country reveal the scale of Idaho's volcanic terrain beyond the principal visitor loop.

photo.alt: A close-up shot of a folded, waving sea of lava rock, with mountains in the far distance.

liri.description: Explore 15,288 acres of waterfalls, forested uplands, and sheer sandstone bluffs along a river flowing atop Lookout Mountain. Canyon overlooks and boulder-strewn pools reveal a distinctive Southern Appalachian landscape.

photo.alt: Fall Season in the Canyon

moja.description: Explore 1.6 million acres of Mojave Desert mountains, dunes, volcanic terrain, and Joshua tree habitat. This vast preserve also protects desert tortoises and traces of ten thousand years of human connection with the desert.

photo.alt: Kelso Dunes with rays of light coming through the clouds. Mountains in the background..

tapr.description: Walk roughly 10,900 acres of surviving tallgrass prairie in the Kansas Flint Hills, where a bison herd helps sustain the grassland. Open horizons and historic ranch places connect a rare ecosystem with generations of human use.

photo.alt: fall wildflowers at the preserve

timu.description: Explore roughly 46,000 acres of salt marshes, coastal dunes, and hardwood hammocks with a human history reaching back some 6,000 years. Fort Caroline and Kingsley Plantation connect this estuary landscape with colonial encounter and the lives of enslaved people.

photo.alt: slave cabins made of tabby with wooden roofs

vall.description: Explore 88,900 acres of mountain meadows and meandering streams inside a volcanic depression fourteen miles wide. This ancient caldera provides habitat for elk and Gunnison's prairie dogs alongside ancestral homelands and historic ranch country.

photo.alt: Scattered clouds over landscape view of winding river and brown grasslands

chch.description: Explore the wooded battlefield and commanding heights where armies fought for Chattanooga in 1863. A Confederate victory at Chickamauga was followed by a Union breakthrough that opened a gateway into the South.

photo.alt: Kelley Cabin

frsp.description: Explore four Civil War battle landscapes around Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, the Wilderness, and Spotsylvania. Preserved fields and historic places reveal the enormous cost borne by soldiers and nearby civilians.

photo.alt: A line of four cannons placed in front of crescent shaped earthen gun pits.

gett.description: Follow ridges, fields, and monuments across the landscape of the Civil War's bloodiest battle. The Union victory ended Lee's second invasion of the North and gave Abraham Lincoln the setting for the Gettysburg Address.

photo.alt: A canon sits in front of an equestrian statue.

guco.description: Walk the wooded battlefield where Greene's and Cornwallis's armies fought on March 15, 1781. The encounter at this small courthouse community changed the course of the Revolution's Southern Campaign.

photo.alt: Bronze and granite monument of General Nathanael Greene on horseback
photo.credit: NPS Photo 【4†Image: Hoskins' House and Kitchen Located on the Grounds of the Colonial Heritage Center】 Hoskins' House and Kitchen Located on the Grounds of the Colonial Heritage Center

hobe.description: Explore the Tallapoosa River bend where Andrew Jackson's army attacked Red Stick Creek defenses on March 27, 1814. The battle's devastating losses and ensuing land cession reshaped the Creek homeland and the southeastern United States.

photo.alt: Sunlight shining on back-lit leaves on a branch.

kimo.description: Follow a wooded ridge where patriot forces won an important Revolutionary victory on October 7, 1780. The battlefield reveals a turning point in the struggle for the southern colonies.

photo.alt: An oval gravestone for Maj Patrick Ferguson is in front of his stone covered grave.

peri.description: Explore 4,400 acres where more than 23,000 soldiers fought on March 7–8, 1862. The preserved battlefield reveals a struggle for Missouri and a pivotal moment in the Civil War west of the Mississippi.

photo.alt: A reconstructed Elkhorn Tavern.

shil.description: Explore the Shiloh and Corinth battle landscapes, where the Civil War's western campaigns left a staggering human cost. Fields, woods, and preserved historic places connect military decisions with the experiences of those who fought.

photo.alt: Ruggles Battery at Shiloh

vick.description: Follow the defensive landscape surrounding the Mississippi River city that both sides considered a key to victory. Fortifications and monuments reveal the campaign and siege that changed the Civil War's course.

photo.alt: Union cannon aimed at Confederate lines

blue.description: Explore a 10.5-mile protected reach of the Bluestone River through a rugged Appalachian gorge. Wooded slopes and riverside routes reveal a landscape rich in habitats and shaped by flowing water.

photo.alt: Bluestone River

buff.description: Follow 135 miles of free-flowing river through the Ozarks, from rapids to quiet pools beneath massive bluffs. Established in 1972, Buffalo National River protects a rare undammed river landscape in the lower forty-eight states.

photo.alt: A large bluff shelter near Buffalo Point.

dela.description: Explore the Middle Delaware's forty-mile river corridor through Delaware Water Gap's wooded ridges and valley. Paddling routes and riverside stops reveal a free-flowing landscape shared by Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

photo.alt: View of the Delaware River cutting between two low mountain peaks

losa.description: Explore the lower St. Croix's wooded riverbanks and historic river towns. This retained inventory entry covers a lower river corridor with multiple access points, rather than a single park entrance.

photo.alt: A blue river winds through a valley lined with trees in autumn color.

mnrr.description: Explore two free-flowing stretches of the Missouri that together preserve roughly one hundred miles of river country. Sandbars, banks, and broad water offer a glimpse of a river landscape transformed elsewhere by dams.

photo.alt: Aerial view of the Missouri River and surrounding landscape.

niob.description: Follow the Niobrara through a valley of waterfalls, wooded slopes, and changing habitats. Canoeing, kayaking, and riverside walks reveal an unexpectedly varied landscape within Nebraska's northern plains.

photo.alt: A beautiful, if short, waterfall empties into the side of the Niobrara NSR.

obri.description: Explore a rugged river gorge on the Cumberland Plateau, where steep sandstone walls rise above moving water. Paddling routes and overlooks reveal the meeting of rivers, rock, and forest.

photo.alt: Obed in Fall

ozar.description: Explore the clear, spring-fed Current and Jacks Fork rivers through the Ozark landscape. Hundreds of freshwater springs, caves, and places such as Alley Mill add depth to paddling and riverside walks.

photo.alt: Sunset picture with high vantage point overlooking river with fall colors and sun setting in distanc

rigr.description: Follow a 196-mile free-flowing reach of the Rio Grande through desert expanses and layered-rock canyons. Remote river journeys reveal a borderland landscape that rewards careful preparation and self-reliance.

photo.alt: Canoeing Boquillas Canyon

sacn.description: Paddle through forested country along the St. Croix and Namekagon rivers, which together offer more than two hundred miles of protected riverway. Historic towns and trails create other ways to explore the banks.

photo.alt: A blue river winds through a valley lined with trees in autumn color.

upde.description: Follow the Delaware through rapids, quiet pools, rolling hills, and riverfront villages. Paddling and fishing places reveal a free-flowing river corridor shared by New York and Pennsylvania.

photo.alt: a view of the Delaware River

apis.description: Explore twenty-one Lake Superior islands and twelve miles of mainland shoreline within the Ojibwe homeland. Sea caves, beaches, and historic lighthouses give this northern archipelago its distinctive character.

photo.alt: Photograph of Lake Superior sandstone rock stack under a blue sky.

piro.description: Explore Lake Superior's sculpted sandstone cliffs, beaches, waterfalls, and dunes. Inland lakes and deep forest add quieter terrain behind a shoreline continually shaped by the great lake.

photo.alt: Golden and orange trees line a sandstone cliff rising above a beach on a cloudy autumn day

slbe.description: Climb into high dune country above Lake Michigan, where bluffs rise as much as 450 feet. Beaches, forests, inland lakes, and historic farmsteads connect broad water views with a layered coastal history.

photo.alt: An overlook of two blue lakes surrounded by trees with fall leaves

anti.description: Follow fields and lanes where twelve hours of fighting on September 17, 1862, left about 23,000 soldiers killed, wounded, or missing. The battle stopped Lee's first northern invasion and preceded Lincoln's preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

photo.alt: luminaries placed by Maryland Monument with dramatic orange red clouds

biho.description: Walk the landscape where U.S. troops attacked a sleeping nimíipuu camp in August 1877. The battlefield preserves a place of loss and remembrance for the Nez Perce people and all who were caught in the fighting.

photo.alt: Multiple tepee poles and a river are silhouetted against a dawn sky.

brcr.description: Explore the crossroads associated with a Confederate victory under Nathan Bedford Forrest. The compact memorial landscape introduces a battle whose tactical result and longer-term consequences told different stories.

photo.alt: Two large trees and a flagpole flying an American flag overlooking a stone monument and cannons

cowp.description: Walk a former pasturing ground where Daniel Morgan's army enveloped British forces in a decisive Revolutionary encounter. The open battlefield helps reveal how a carefully planned maneuver became a patriot victory.

photo.alt: The sun is coming up on the battlefield in the direction that the Americans would have been facing.

fodo.description: Explore the river fortress whose surrender on February 16, 1862, brought Ulysses S. Grant national attention. The Union victory opened a route into Tennessee and quickly changed the military balance in the West.

photo.alt: The View from the Upper River Battery

fone.description: Explore the meadow landscape where fighting in 1754 opened the French and Indian War. The site connects a young George Washington with a larger struggle among British, French, and Indigenous powers.

photo.alt: Circular stockade in the middle of a meadow. Dramatic clouds build in the blue sky.

kemo.description: Explore 2,965 acres of wooded mountain and preserved battlefield from the 1864 Atlanta Campaign. Trails and historic ground connect wide-ranging views with the armies' maneuvers and fighting.

photo.alt: Cannon with front field and Visitor Center in background.

mana.description: Walk the fields above Bull Run where armies fought in July 1861 and again in August 1862. The landscape reveals how the expectation of a short war gave way to repeated, costly conflict.

photo.alt: Red sandstone obelisk surrounded by post and rail fence.

mono.description: Explore farms and riverbanks where outnumbered Union troops fought on July 9, 1864. Their delaying action bought time for reinforcements to reach Washington during a Confederate advance on the capital.

photo.alt: Federal style house with trees behind it during the fall season.

mocr.description: Follow the creek-side battlefield where patriot forces waited beyond a partially dismantled bridge on February 27, 1776. The brief encounter became an important early Revolutionary victory in North Carolina.

photo.alt: Cannon on a hill on a winter day. American flag to the left of the cannon

pete.description: Explore the ground of a 292-day siege that cut supplies to Petersburg and Richmond. Earthworks and separate battlefield sites reveal the campaign's immense cost and its role in the collapse of Lee's army.

photo.alt: Pictured is the front of the brick visitor center under a cloudless blue sky.

rich.description: Explore battlefields, earthworks, and historic places surrounding the Confederate capital. The park connects military campaigns with the factories, hospitals, and civilian lives caught up in Richmond's wartime importance.

photo.alt: Earthen trenches running through a wooded area of bare trees and fallen autumn leaves.

rira.description: Explore the landscape of the January 1813 River Raisin battles and their aftermath. The site connects a major British and Indigenous victory with the later policies of removal and assimilation imposed on Native nations.

photo.alt: Painting of the Battle of the River Raisin

stri.description: Walk fields and wooded ground where the Battle of Stones River began on the last day of 1862. The Union's gains came at a terrible cost to the soldiers and communities whose lives were changed here.

photo.alt: The sun rises behind a green field with a cannon in the foreground.

tupe.description: Pause at the memorial ground of the July 1864 fighting around Tupelo. The campaign involved United States Colored Troops and helped keep Confederate forces away from important Union railroads in Tennessee.

photo.alt: The monument with a cannon

wicr.description: Explore the rolling battlefield of August 10, 1861, the first major Civil War battle west of the Mississippi. The costly Southern victory brought national attention to the conflict in Missouri.

photo.alt: Men in reproduction uniforms talk around a campfire

ciro.description: Explore granite spires and rock formations that California Trail emigrants likened to a city. Climbing routes, walking paths, and historic traces connect unusual geology with the journeys of nineteenth-century travelers.

photo.alt: Snow dusted granite formations jut up from a mountainous juniper covered landscape.

ebla.description: Walk a Salish Sea landscape of working farmland, coastal bluffs, and historic settlement. The reserve preserves the intertwined agricultural and cultural traditions of Native and Euro-American communities.

photo.alt: View from the Bluff Overlook

sacr.description: Look toward the island where a French expedition endured the deadly winter of 1604–1605. The mainland site interprets the settlement attempt and the Indigenous aid that helped survivors recover when spring returned.

photo.alt: View of the drive into Saint Croix Island International Historic Site.
